reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A subepidermal blistering disease defined by linear IgA deposition along the basement membrane zone on direct immunofluorescence

The childhood form (chronic bullous disease of childhood) classically shows annular or rosette-like clusters of tense blisters ('string of pearls' or 'cluster of jewels') around the perineum and lower trunk
The adult form is more heterogeneous and can mimic bullous pemphigoid or dermatitis herpetiformis
Frequently drug-induced, with vancomycin being the most commonly implicated agent; withdrawal often leads to resolution
Target antigens are typically fragments of BP180 (the LAD-1/LABD97 ectodomain) within the basement membrane zone
Unlike dermatitis herpetiformis it is not associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy and does not respond to a gluten-free diet
Dapsone is a mainstay of treatment given the neutrophil-rich subepidermal infiltrate
reference.pathophysiology: Linear IgA bullous dermatosis is an immune-mediated subepidermal blistering disease in which IgA autoantibodies bind antigens in the basement membrane zone, most often cleaved ectodomain fragments of BP180 (LAD-1/LABD97). Antibody deposition along the dermo-epidermal junction recruits neutrophils, whose enzymatic and inflammatory activity separates the epidermis from the dermis to form tense subepidermal blisters. The characteristic linear (rather than granular) IgA pattern distinguishes it from dermatitis herpetiformis. Many adult cases are triggered by drugs, particularly vancomycin, in which the aberrant immune response abates once the drug is stopped.
additionalDifferentials: Bullous erythema multiforme / Stevens-Johnson syndrome (especially in children)
additionalInvestigations: Perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence showing linear IgA at the basement membrane zone
Lesional biopsy for histology demonstrating a subepidermal blister with neutrophils
Indirect immunofluorescence for circulating IgA basement membrane antibodies
Salt-split skin study to localise antibody binding, typically to the epidermal (roof) side
Detailed drug history, especially recent vancomycin exposure
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase level before starting dapsone
redFlags: Extensive blistering with mucosal or ocular involvement risking scarring
Recent initiation of a culprit drug requiring prompt withdrawal
Haemolysis or methaemoglobinaemia as complications of dapsone therapy
reference.prognosis: The childhood form frequently remits spontaneously within a few years, and drug-induced adult cases usually resolve after the trigger is withdrawn; idiopathic adult disease may be more persistent but generally responds well to dapsone.
pitfalls: Confusing it with dermatitis herpetiformis and instituting an unnecessary gluten-free diet
Overlooking a drug trigger, particularly vancomycin, that would resolve on withdrawal
Starting dapsone without checking glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status
Missing mucosal involvement that requires closer monitoring for scarring
management: Identify and withdraw any implicated drug, especially vancomycin, as drug-induced disease frequently resolves once the trigger is stopped
First-line pharmacotherapy for idiopathic disease is dapsone, checking glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status beforehand to avoid haemolysis
Use sulfapyridine or add systemic corticosteroids where dapsone is insufficient or not tolerated, sometimes in combination
Provide skin and wound care for blisters and erosions, with attention to preventing and treating secondary infection
Monitor for dapsone-related haemolytic anaemia and methaemoglobinaemia during treatment
Reassure in the childhood form (chronic bullous disease of childhood), which frequently remits spontaneously over a few years
Refer to dermatology for direct-immunofluorescence-guided diagnosis and management
